newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters UPS strike in second day with no talks set.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters UPS strike in second day with no talks set.

text.p: The strike across America against United Parcel Service dragged into a second day Tuesday, with no talks scheduled between management and the Teamsters union despite renewed efforts by a federal mediator.
As the strike idled UPS facilities for a second day, it spelled more trouble for American businesses and consumers, who were forced to seek other ways to ship their packages and documents.

Thousands of members of the Teamsters union, including drivers, package sorters and loaders, walked picket lines from Maine to California, as about 45,000 UPS managers and non-union workers tried to keep the system operating.

The world's largest parcel delivery company, which lost $50 million during a partial one-day strike in 1994, said 10 percent or less of its usual 12 million packages a day were being delivered and that only a few facilities were operating normally. It stopped taking orders from consumers and shifted its focus to express and international shipments.
"If you're looking to send something to grandma, this is not the time," UPS spokeswoman Kristen Petrella said.

Union officials said the strike had crippled the company. "UPS is pretty much buttoned up. Packages in the system are drying up and the strike appears to be virtually 100 percent effective," Teamsters spokesman Rand Wilson said.

The 185,000 Teamsters who sort and load packages, haul shipments and drive the company's familiar brown vans and trucks account for two thirds of the work force at the company, which is based in Atlanta.

Deliveries inside and between European countries remained unaffected by the strike. But Petrella said UPS was no longer guaranteeing deliveries on parcels bound overseas from inside the United States.
At picket lines, five more Teamsters were arrested for violence, bringing the number of arrests near UPS facilities to more than a dozen, police said.

With the union and UPS far apart on the use of part-time workers, pay, pensions, and other issues, the White House reiterated that it was unlikely President Bill Clinton would intervene because the strike did not pose a threat to the nation's economic health.
But federal mediator John Calhoun Wells said he would talk to both sides in a bid to get management and labour back to the bargaining table to discuss their differences.
"I am going to be in touch with both sides this morning as I was yesterday morning and yesterday afternoon and we just have to see where it goes," he told CNN.
Both sides said they were ready to talk but also accused the other side of obstinance.

The walkout, the first national strike in UPS' 90-year history, is also the largest in the United States this decade. It pits a wealthy service company using more part-time workers against a union whose members are angry about the practice, as well as other issues. Part-time jobs pay $9 an hour on average after two years vs. $20 an hour for full-time jobs at UPS.
The strike is also a gamble for Teamster President Ron Carey, who is facing powerful opposition in the union and allegations of fund-raising abuses in his re-election campaign last year.
Meanwhile, other labour organisations were weighing how they would react to the strike.
The executive council of the AFL-CIO was expected to meet soon in Chicago to decide whether to help the Teamsters union replenish its depleted strike fund.
The Teamsters also sent representatives to Europe to speak with European unions that were expected to hold demonstrations in support of the strike.

The Independent Pilots Association, which represents 2,000 UPS pilots, was still supporting the strike by keeping members off the job. The company refused to provide hotel accommodations to 300 members stranded by the walkout.

"The IPA must be deluded to think the company would be responsible for its travel and hotel expenses after they withheld their services from UPS," said Ken Shapiro, a spokesman for the UPS Air Group in Louisville, Ky.
UPS consolidated its air shipment services at the Louisville hub, which on Monday night handled 40 UPS flights piloted by managers and 29 chartered flights, 30 percent of its normal capacity.
